President Donald J. Trump, flanked by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Secretary of Interior Doug Burgum, attends a roundtable in August for the American mining industry in Washington, D.C. Credit: White House Photo by Joyce N. Boghosian
Posted By: Colin McClelland November 2, 2026
“There is no better time to be mining in the United States.”
For Rich Nolan, president and CEO of the National Mining Association, President Donald Trump’s second administration has transformed Washington’s relationship with an industry that for decades complained of being ignored or obstructed.
Less than two years into Trump’s term, the federal government has pushed projects through accelerated permitting, taken equity stakes in mineral companies, offered price floors and offtakes, expanded loans and grants and put mineral security near the centre of U.S. economic and defence policy.
Project Vault has also moved from concept to physical stockpile. In October, commodities trader Mercuria delivered 12,000 tonnes of copper from the Democratic Republic of Congo to warehouses on the U.S. Gulf and East coasts, the first disclosed copper delivery to the initiative.
“That’s a sea change in the U.S. government’s posture,” Nolan told The Northern Miner . “The industry is in a markedly different position than we were just a year ago.”
Unruly backdrop
But Trump’s mining push sits inside a far less predictable presidency. His administration has escalated trade disputes, including a damaging tariff fight with Canada, the United States’ largest export market and one of its most important mineral suppliers.
Trump, who has long criticized U.S. involvement in “endless wars,” has also committed American forces to a lengthy conflict with Iran. His administration has simultaneously rolled back environmental protections and accelerated project approvals, drawing legal challenges from states and environmental groups.
Against that backdrop, four industry and policy specialists interviewed by The Northern Miner offered sharply different assessments of the mining record.
Reed Blakemore, director of research and programs at the Global Energy Center, part of non-partisan think tank the Atlantic Council, called the expanded federal toolkit “genuinely new and genuinely constructive,” but warned that project-by-project support alone can’t build supply chains capable of competing with China.
Zahava Urecki, a senior policy analyst at the Bipartisan Policy Center in Washington, credited the administration with putting mineral security front and centre, while questioning whether its financing tools, processing strategy and executive actions will prove durable.
Aaron Mintzes, senior policy counsel at U.S. environmental group Earthworks, sees the same changes much more critically, arguing that government equity stakes create conflicts and faster permitting has weakened environmental and Indigenous protections.
Yet all four converge on one point: the experiment is unfinished. China still dominates crucial processing steps, and whether Washington’s new mining policy produces durable supply chains remains the test.
Rich Nolan
“The approach the administration has taken to improve the competitiveness of U.S. mining is an all hands on deck, all the above approach,” Nolan said.
“While we’ve really seen a massive global awakening to the scale and urgency of the minerals challenge, this administration is actually moving aggressively to address it.”
“Efforts to streamline permitting and bring more transparency and certainty to the process are bearing fruit. We’re seeing projects now move through the FAST-41 permitting program with far more coordination and support than we have seen traditionally.
“That’s very encouraging but there’s no question we need congressional action on permitting to affect the kind of sweeping change that’s required for this moment.”
The bipartisan permitting deal under consideration in the Senate would maintain rigorous review while setting firm timelines, reducing duplication and addressing litigation that can delay projects for years, Nolan said.
“There is a recognition that there is no single solution to breaking China’s hold on our minerals supply chains. The U.S. must embrace the enormity of the challenge and bring new tools to the fight.”
China’s state subsidies and dominance of mines and processing have created an uneven playing field that requires a more ambitious U.S. response, Nolan said.
“Historically, the U.S. government understood the critical importance of building and supporting domestic productive capacity. I think we’re seeing a rediscovery and reinvention of many the tools that made the U.S. a mineral superpower in the 20th century.”
“While we’ve taken important steps to reshore our domestic industry, change can’t happen overnight. The lead times for mining are historically long, and China has a two-decade lead that it’s not going to give up willingly.”
“So much of the success or failure of today’s mineral security effort will come down to follow through. Are today’s efforts a beginning of a new era for American mining or a blip and then a return to the status quo?”
“We’re already seeing shovels in the ground on new projects and ribbons being cut to start production on mines that for too long were awaiting final approvals.”
“I don’t think there’s any going back to the way things were before. And that’s a remarkable achievement.”
Reed Blakemore
“I think the toolkit that this administration has deployed over the past two years is genuinely new and genuinely constructive.”
Blakemore contrasted the approach with the previous administration’s greater reliance on tax credits and grants.
“I think the move towards equity stakes, the exploration of price floors, offtakes, and kind of reserves, I think that begins to create the appropriate government interventions … that actually begin to improve the economics of supply chain activity in the United States.”
FAST-41 designations have helped some projects, but the permitting environment remains “quite sticky,” Blakemore said.
“It’s how permitting can get gummed up as it moves through the regulatory and court process.”
“We fast tracked certain parts of the permitting process, but ultimately, once it gets to the proverbial courthouse door, it can still get really, really slow.”
“It’s an interesting tool. It’s an incredibly powerful tool. It is an evolution of U.S. industrial policy that we haven’t seen yet.”
Limited equity positions can help strategic assets survive markets skewed by foreign state support, but there are limits, Blakemore said.
“The United States is not going to secure its critical mineral supply chains by trying to out subsidise China.”
“Can limited equity stakes provide a de-risking tool needed to make certain assets help certain assets get off the ground as a short-term solution? Absolutely, but I don’t think we will see equity stakes be the core pillar of long-term supply chain strategy.”
Allied cooperation is “absolutely critical” and the administration has matured from believing in domestic self-sufficiency, Blakemore said.
Canada matters because of geography and shared values, Europe can help aggregate demand, and Japan has important midstream technical capacity, he said.
Success should eventually be measurable through a partner-based trade regime, coordinated offtakes and price support, and an alternative for mineral-rich countries dependent on Chinese capital, Blakemore said.
“The United States isn’t necessarily going to be able to compete on speed of capital. So, what is the compelling alternative that the United States can offer those countries?”
Zahava Urecki
“I’d say broadly to answer that question is just their focus on mineral security writ large.”
Urecki pointed to Project Vault, executive orders and Washington’s willingness to look beyond traditional grants and loans.
“Just key is having minerals top of mind is huge, just given … where the supply chain struggles are and how China’s been so dominant.”
Many of the policy changes will take years to judge, she cautioned.
“A lot of these moves, we won’t really know the true effect or how effective they were until years in advance.”
Projects are clearly receiving more federal attention, though permitting is not her main area of expertise, Urecki said.
“They have put a focus on this. You have been seeing projects get a lot of attention and trying to move them forward.”
She was reluctant to identify a definitive example where federal action has already transformed a project’s path into construction.
“The equity deals are new, not brand new, but they were not something that’s been utilised often.”
Urecki called the approach creative but said questions remain about the terms, funding sources and strategy for deciding which minerals or companies should receive support.
“It’s nice to see that they’re taking a unique approach to this and trying to use all the tools in the toolbox.”
On whether the equity deals themselves prove to be the right approach, she said it is “still to be determined.”
Domestic mining by itself cannot solve the supply-chain problem, Urecki said.
“We can mine all we want, but if we can’t process here, then it’s what’s the point? It’s all going to China anyway.”
Washington needs mechanisms that make U.S. processing commercially viable when Chinese supply drives prices lower, while also prioritizing among an expanding list of critical minerals rather than spreading federal resources too thinly, she said.
The administration deserves credit for making mineral security a central policy issue, but durable policy will require cooperation with Congress and allies, Urecki said.
“Any executive orders are tough to have that staying power, just given … administration changes, people wanting to make their own mark.”
Aaron Mintzes
“There are two of the greatest changes. One is on the money side, the decision to take equity stakes in mines … and then the second is the evisceration of the National Environmental Policy Act regulations.”
Shortened reviews have reduced opportunities for the public to understand and comment on federal mining decisions, Mintzes said. He cited a uranium mine permitted in 14 days and a lithium exploration proposal with five days for public comment.
Mintzes rejected the premise that U.S. mine permitting is excessively slow.
“No, I don’t accept the premise.”
The median time to permit a hardrock mine on public lands is three years, he said, citing a federal interagency review.
“The permitting process is no obstacle. If anything, current law and permitting helps facilitate mines rather than slow them down. The problem usually is money.”
He also criticized expedited reviews that, in his view, weaken environmental scrutiny and Tribal consultation.
Federal equity stakes create a conflict when the government acts as mine owner, regulator and permitter, Mintzes said.
“An owner might be less interested in, say, paying fines for an environmental regulation.”
He also warned that commodity cycles expose taxpayers to risk and that direct government support can distort competition.
“You have the government picking winners and losers.”
Mintzes rejected the administration’s extraction-heavy response to Chinese dominance.
“I would view the administration’s approach as feckless and weak and submissive.”
The 1872 Mining Law allows foreign as well as domestic companies to acquire mineral claims on public land without enough public benefit, he argued.
Instead, Washington should place more emphasis on processing technology, recycling electronic waste and batteries, and other midstream and downstream capacity, he said.
Asked to assign the administration a grade, Mintzes declined to choose a letter.
Washington is concentrating too heavily on additional extraction when, in his view, the main vulnerabilities lie farther along at midstream and downstream, he said.
“I would just give them an incomplete.”

Public affairs strategists John Ashford and Jared Dubnow examine the political backlash against data centers, the implications for power-sector investment and regulation, and the potential for public opposition to spread to emerging generation technologies.
Data centers have rapidly become a contentious election issue, as concerns over electricity affordability, infrastructure costs, and local development reshape political attitudes toward an industry that states have aggressively courted for investment. The backlash could accelerate state regulation of large electricity loads, regardless of the outcome of the Nov. 3 midterm elections. One reason may be that public sentiment has shifted substantially. Half of Americans now oppose a data center built within three miles of their homes, compared with 28% in January, according to The POLITICO Poll , conducted Oct. 16–19 by PF Global. The political pressure is also visible in state policy. In Texas, Gov. Greg Abbott has directed reviews of data center interconnection requests and permitting, while Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker has called for changes to state data center incentives. In Georgia, two seats on the five-member Public Service Commission are on the Nov. 3 ballot, which creates the possibility of a change in partisan control of the agency that regulates Georgia Power.
Federal permitting reform is also approaching a procedural vote. On Nov. 9, the U.S. Senate is scheduled to vote on cloture on a motion to proceed to H.R. 2347 , the legislative vehicle for a broader permitting reform package. POWER has reported on provisions addressing transmission costs associated with large data center loads, alongside measures intended to accelerate energy infrastructure development.
For John Ashford and Jared Dubnow of The Hawthorn Group , an international public affairs firm, these developments reflect a political shift that began in communities confronting data center siting decisions and is now influencing state and federal policy. Ashford, Hawthorn’s chairman and CEO, co-founded the firm in 1992 after working on political campaigns alongside consultant Matt Reese. Dubnow, a senior vice president, previously worked in Illinois politics, including in the governor’s office and at the Illinois Department of Commerce and Economic Opportunity.
In written responses to POWER ahead of Election Day, the two strategists examined how electricity demand is influencing campaigns, why data center regulation could persist regardless of election outcomes, and how the power industry should prepare for changing political and community expectations. They also warned that developers of emerging generation technologies, including small modular reactors (SMRs), may be underestimating how quickly public attitudes can change.
The following Q&A was conducted jointly in writing. Responses have been edited lightly for style. Brief editorial clarifications appear in brackets.
POWER: What are the most significant energy issues shaping the 2026 midterm elections? How prominently are electricity affordability, grid reliability, data center development, and energy infrastructure featuring in campaigns? Where are these issues resonating most strongly?
Data centers, data centers, and more data centers. In our experience, we’ve never seen an issue take hold so quickly and move from the darling of states and governors to the biggest boogeyman and enemy of the people—according to an October POLITICO poll, half of all Americans would oppose a data center built within three miles of their home. It’s become a third rail of politics. And with data centers, you are really getting affordability, rising electricity costs, not-in-my-backyard opposition (NIMBYism), and the future of our electric grid.
These issues, especially data centers, are playing a role in nearly every major gubernatorial, Senate, and legislative race across the country. And in the states with gubernatorial and/or legislative elections in 2027—including Kentucky, Louisiana, Mississippi, New Jersey, and Virginia [the first three hold gubernatorial elections; New Jersey and Virginia hold legislative elections]—you can bet they’ll be featured prominently, even though many voters have no real idea of the role data centers play in their everyday lives. In some races, it’s the defining feature, but in none is it absent, if only as a talking point on a mailer or TV ad: “I’ll hold data centers accountable; my opponent won’t.” In Georgia, Wisconsin, and Ohio, data centers have become the central issue in the gubernatorial races (Georgia and Wisconsin) and the Senate race (Ohio).
POWER: Which election outcomes could have the greatest consequences for the power industry? Beyond the federal implications, which gubernatorial and state legislative contests could alter utility regulation, resource planning, generation development, and infrastructure permitting? Are there particular states or races the industry should be watching closely?
Georgia is one of the most interesting places because, in addition to the marquee gubernatorial and Senate races, two Public Service Commission (PSC) commissioners are up for election. This follows a 2025 election in which two Democratic candidates won, and for the first time in about two decades, Democrats might actually have a majority on the PSC. This will have major implications for data center generation and how Georgia Power manages the state’s electric grid and generation.
Another consequential election is Wisconsin, where not just the governor is a toss-up, but the legislature is, too. Democrats have a real shot at a power shift and a trifecta, likely bringing on a new wave of anti-data-center regulations, pro-renewable mandates, and policies to curb rising electricity costs.
Finally, Texas looms large on both the state and federal levels. Gov. Greg Abbott has turned on a dime in a few months, from urging vast data center construction to bringing it to a halt. Similarly, the Senate race, pitting Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton against James Talarico, will have major implications not only for the balance of power, but for what kind of partner companies will find in Washington come 2027. Either way, the political reality and pushback in the Lone Star State will have real implications for both data centers and utilities.
POWER: How should the power sector distinguish political rhetoric from consequential policy shifts? Regardless of which party controls Congress or individual states, which regulatory or legislative priorities are likely to persist? Which could change direction significantly?
We may sound like a broken record, but data center regulation is likely here to stay. And it’s not an issue that was born in Congress or in statehouses. It emanates from community opposition groups that have reacted—whether right or wrong—to community siting decisions by data center developers. And now that the trend has taken hold, it’s very difficult to put the genie back in the bottle. The most responsible, community-responsive data center developer is finding that the industry as a whole has been branded as toxic. Too many campaigns and candidates, in response to community opposition, ran on holding them accountable, and now they will have to do something. We fully expect data center regulation, whether around bring-your-own generation, large-load tariffs, or something similar, to be on the menu in every state. And for at least the next year or two, these issues will continue.
Beyond that, keep an eye on permitting reform: will it pass out of the Senate Nov. 9, and what will the implications be, including potential pushback from states that feel the federal government is getting too close for comfort in regulating them? Beyond that, however, I would expect the power industry to widely support a measure that fundamentally allows them to approve projects faster, deliver electrons more easily, and mitigate the massive interconnection backlog that has hampered the industry for years now.
Editor’s note: The Senate is scheduled to vote Nov. 9 on cloture on the motion to proceed to H.R. 2347, which Senate leaders are using as the legislative vehicle for the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act . Final passage would require further floor votes.
POWER: Data center demand has become a major political and economic issue. How is it influencing electoral debates over electricity prices, infrastructure development, and cost allocation between large customers and existing ratepayers? Are political leaders changing their approach to data center investment?
Just turn on the TV or open any newspaper; data centers are the defining energy and infrastructure issue right now. They touch every power and energy topic—generation, costs, transmission permitting, land use, environmental and water concerns. And while there is real anger over data centers, they’re also likely becoming the boogeyman for other energy-related issues they aren’t directly responsible for, such as rising electricity costs. Take transmission, for example: the entire transmission system needs a major upgrade, which will cost billions of dollars, much of which ratepayers are on the hook for. Should a data center really have to pay for the entire system upgrade because we have a half-century-old system (or more in most cases) that can’t handle new load growth? Probably not, but they are the easy scapegoat to pin all of our problems—and cost increases—on.
And so yes, we’ve seen a massive shift in how leaders approach data centers. Take two incumbent governors who are on almost every issue at opposite ends of the political spectrum: Gov. JB Pritzker in Illinois and Gov. Greg Abbott in Texas. Both were data center cheerleaders, leading the charge to recruit more, offer incentives, and position their states as the next technological leaders. Yet, in 12 months or less, both have called for a pause on state incentives and said the 2027 session (or sooner) needs new data center regulations and reforms.
POWER: Several states are reconsidering regulated utility ownership of generation as concerns about resource adequacy intensify. How might the election influence these debates, competitive electricity markets, generation investment, and long-term resource planning?
The election may change who’s in control, but the discussion is decades old, with arguments no different today than they were 30 years ago, when markets and states were (in some cases) restructuring into a more competitive system. And the response, same as 30 years ago, will be wrapped around “affordability.” The difference today is social media and transparency. The ability to know what’s going on today is based on real-time knowledge. It’s a world of instant knowledge and gratification. And while we can’t solve the problem of affordability and building new generation in real time, we do need to solve it more quickly.
Everyone wants a hand in it—the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC), state commissions and governors, state legislators and, of course, local officials and communities. And they all have a role. Utilities want to build their own generation, saying they have access to lower-cost capital. Third-party developers want to compete to build generation, noting that competition disciplines cost. Same as it ever was. The issue is who can bring these projects online most efficiently and cost-effectively. There is a case to be made for both.
In the restructured markets, there is no question that addressing queue bottlenecks and bringing on more generation sooner is critical. For too long, these issues have been allowed to fester. In more regulated systems where utilities can self-build, the issue isn’t just ensuring that construction is done in the most cost-effective way possible, but doing it faster.
And in many of these cases, federal and state regulatory commissions are going to have to call the “balls and strikes” more quickly, recognizing that it’s not just speed to power but understanding, incorporating, and respecting local communities and their concerns—and addressing those concerns in a real, transparent, and collaborative way, while recognizing that talk and “just saying no” produce delay and won’t solve the problem.
Public officials have to recognize it. Communities do, too. Developers need to engage communities and local officials sooner and with more information, or opponents will fill the void with “just say no.” Regulators, elected leaders, and advocacy groups also need to do a better job explaining the need and purpose and the collective benefit that more generation and an upgraded electric system will have for us all. It will take courage and a willingness to engage during a period when engagement is often challenging, profiles in courage are harder to find, and public officials spend more time worrying about reelection or reappointment.
POWER: Power projects require years of planning, financing, permitting, and construction. Which political or regulatory changes could most directly affect capital allocation and project execution? How should companies account for these risks in long-term investment decisions?
A better question is: given the ever-changing political and regulatory environment, which is not necessarily purely partisan, how can companies best plan their long-term investment decisions proactively? And to that, we’d say relationship building. Across the board, companies need to invest better in the entire project. That includes relationship building and local-level research, planning for political changes, shoring up friends and allies on both sides of the aisle, and creating opportunities to engage early on policy decisions that may impact long-term investments. Companies do an incredible job of planning and forecasting the investment. They should do the same level of planning and forecasting for the political and regulatory environment, at the local, state, and federal levels.
POWER: Looking toward 2027, which emerging political, regulatory, or public-opinion shifts should utilities, independent power producers, equipment suppliers, and developers be preparing for? Are there risks the industry may be underestimating?
As the data center question is addressed, a massive buildout of transmission and generation will soon follow. And we’re potentially on the cusp of new forms of generation, from small modular reactors (SMRs) to renewable natural gas [as a power-generation fuel] to geothermal. While there’s a lot of excitement in the market today, and seemingly little opposition or even excitement for these new technologies, we think the market likely underestimates how quickly sentiment and political winds can change. It happened with data centers, and it is likely to happen with other technology. Let’s discuss SMRs as just one example. We only need to look back to the massive opposition to nuclear energy in the 1960s and 1970s to see how controversial it can be. One small potential issue at the first or second test facility can set off a wave of new opposition across the country.

Dodge Recalls 2026 Durango SUV Over Potentially Damaged Taillight Wiring Harness Terminals
66 photos
Photo: Dodge
Stellantis North America has identified a taillight-related issue affecting only a handful of 2026 model year Durango sport utility vehicles. This campaign, which is referred to as 26V701 by the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration, is not related to the recent extended warranty coverage announcement for the rear light assembly on 2018 through 2024 models.
Older models are susceptible to water infiltration that causes the LED circuitry to corrode. Potential outcomes include dimming, partial failure, or complete light failure. Customers who paid for repairs or replacement of the taillamp assembly out of pocket can file a reimbursement claim. 2018 to 2024 Dodge Durango vehicles that have passed the five-year coverage are provided with a 6-month window from the notification date for eligible repairs.
Turning our attention back to the safety recall, which is a different animal from a customer satisfaction program that covers the rear lights, the recall documentation reveals that bent terminals in the wiring harness may be damaged. Obviously enough, such damage prevents the rear assembly from lighting up as intended, leaving following drivers to guess whether the affected vehicle is braking or not.
Subject vehicles were produced in the United States from January 5 through February 20 this year, and the Dodge brand estimates that only 3 percent of the 13,330-strong population actually contains the defect. Even so, all have to be inspected for bent terminals because reduced visibility increases the risk of a crash. Also worth noting, this defect goes against FMVSS 108.
Said federal motor vehicle safety standard requires completely functional taillamps, stop lamps, backup lamps, and turn signal lamps. Not displaying the required lighting is a noncompliance in the NHTSA's eyes, and Dodge is much obliged to please the safety boffins. The affected components are identified under two part numbers, which are supplied by Michigan's Ventra Greenwich Holdings.
Photo: Dodge 68272126AC and 68272127AC are the part numbers in question, and the Mopar eStore lists both as being compatible with 2014 through 2027 models. Unfortunately for affected customers and prospective customers, the recall documentation fails to explain what caused the terminals to bend in the first place.
Although the root cause remains a mystery for us, a clue lies in the remedy. According to Stellantis North America, dealers are to replace suspect taillamps with new units featuring "terminals with the correct dimensions." Reading between the lines, either the supplier or a sub-supplier is to blame for the potentially bent terminals.
The dealer inspection procedure, which is also available on the NHTSA 's website, tells Dodge service techs to check the production date labels on both taillamps. Anything produced from December 16, 2025, through January 27, 2026, should be considered suspect. Of course, replacement lights come at no charge to affected owners and lessees.
Stellantis North America does not describe any separate wiring harness repair in the dealer inspection procedure document. FCA US LLC's safety and regulatory team started looking into this matter back on June 16, 2026. Through September 2026, the company reviewed a bunch of records while also working with the engineering department to establish the root cause and vehicle population.
Suspect vehicles are now searchable on the NHTSA's website by VIN. Customer notification letters, however, will have to wait until December 3, 2026.

Posted By: Henry Lazenby November 2, 2026
Chile’s copper commission has cut its production forecasts for the world’s largest producer and raised its 2027 price outlook by 17% as mines struggle to recover lost output.
Cochilco raised its average copper price forecast for next year to $5.95 (C$8.32) per lb. from $5.10 in releases issued Friday. It now expects Chilean output to fall 8.4% this year, compared with the 2.6% decline projected in August.
“The [global] surpluses we project are small and can change with operational delays or higher-than-expected consumption,” Executive Vice-President Claudia Rodríguez said in a price announcement Friday.
The projected surplus of refined metal leaves little room for further supply disruptions. Demand just 1% above next year’s forecast would erase the surplus and create a deficit of about 65,000 tonnes if supply stayed unchanged, according to calculations based on Cochilco’s figures.
BMO Capital Markets analysts Helen Amos and George Heppel said the downgrade could leave Chile with its weakest annual copper production in more than two decades.
Chile’s decline
Cochilco raised its average price forecast for this year to $6.18 per lb. from $5.95. It still expects prices to ease 3.7% next year as supply recovers, but that decline depends on mines meeting their production plans and metal reaching consumers.
Chile is expected to produce 4.94 million tonnes of the red metal this year and 5.08 million tonnes next year, down from the agency’s August forecasts of 5.27 million and 5.55 million tonnes, respectively.
The country produced 3.63 million tonnes in this year’s first nine months, down 8.5% from a year earlier. BHP’s (ASX, LSE, NYSE: BHP) Escondida and Spence operations, together with state-owned Codelco, accounted for 77% of the net national decline .
Cochilco points to lower ore grades, maintenance and interruptions affecting both the amount of material processed and the copper recovered. Reaching even the reduced annual forecast requires monthly production of about 434,000 tonnes in the fourth quarter, 7.6% above the average through September.
Cochilco forecasts global mine production will rebound 3.4% next year to 24.08 million tonnes after slipping 0.6% this year. Chile and the Democratic Republic of Congo would supply about 37% of that increase, making their recovery central to Cochilco’s market outlook. Chile would still produce 5.7% less copper than in 2025.
Uneven stocks
Cochilco forecasts a refined-copper surplus of 144,000 tonnes this year, equivalent to 0.5% of consumption, widening to 215,000 tonnes next year, or 0.8%. Higher refining output, supported partly by intermediate stocks and recycled material, can coexist with falling mine production, it pointed out.
The location of available metal adds to the strain. In its separate weekly market report, also released Friday, Cochilco recorded 1.05 million tonnes across the three principal exchanges. The U.S. exchange COMEX held almost 70% of the total, while Shanghai Futures Exchange stocks fell 18% during the week to 44,612 tonnes.
China’s Yangshan import premium reached $205 per tonne, while cash copper on the London Metals Exchange traded $210 per tonne above the three-month contract on Thursday. Those premiums reflect the higher cost of obtaining metal for immediate delivery.
Cochilco cautioned that fewer arrivals, shipping delays and contractual supply restrictions helped draw down Chinese stocks. The decline therefore doesn’t establish a broad acceleration in consumption.
Demand offers less reassurance. The BMO analysts warned that AI investment is one of the few engines of industrial growth while construction and autos remain sluggish. A material slowdown in data-centre spending would leave few alternatives to cushion the impact on demand, they said.

In a mid-stage trial, the lower dose of Tiziana’s intranasal monoclonal antibody reduced microglial activation in a specific type of multiple sclerosis. But the path forward remains unclear after the higher dose failed to deliver the same benefit.
Tiziana Life Sciences’ lead candidate significantly reduced a neuroinflammation biomarker in multiple sclerosis at one dose level but failed to beat placebo at a higher dose.
As of Monday’s market open, the biotech’s stock slid 17% to 67 cents per share.
Tiziana’s Phase 2a INFORM-MS trial is testing three-week cycles of foralumab, an anti-CD3 monoclonal antibody delivered intranasally, for patients with non-active secondary progressive multiple sclerosis (na-SPMS). Patients with this form of MS typically experience a gradual worsening of symptoms without relapse or new MRI activity. Patients experience progressive disability and fatigue; no FDA-approved treatments are specifically indicated for na-SPMS.
INFORM-MS met its dual primary endpoints—one safety and one efficacy measure—for 19 patients receiving the 50-µg dose but missed the efficacy endpoint at the 100-µg dose, according to a Monday news release .
At the lower dose, foralumab was tied to a statistically significant reduction in microglial activation at 12 weeks as compared to placebo. Microglia are thought to play a key role in inflammatory responses in MS.
No significant difference was recorded for the 11 patients receiving 100 µg of foralumab, however. Tiziana did not provide specific data behind the results, which were assessed using PET imaging to measure a mitochondrial protein biomarker.
On the safety side, the U.K.- and Boston-based biotech said that the two doses of intranasal foralumab were safe and well tolerated. The most common treatment-emergent adverse events were headache, fall, nasal congestion and runny nose.

On secondary measures, patients receiving foralumab showed improvements in fatigue compared with their own baseline scores, according to Tiziana, and no changes were recorded on a disability progression tracker.
“These results represent a significant milestone for patients with non-active secondary progressive MS, a population with significant unmet need and limited treatment options,” said Tanuja Chitnis, INFORM-MS principal investigator and neurology professor at Harvard Medical School/Brigham and Women’s Hospital, said in the Monday news release. “We consider these findings as encouraging evidence of the biological activity of nasal foralumab in this MS population where at present there are no approved treatments for these patients.”
Tiziana plans to present detailed findings from the trial at an upcoming scientific conference and meet with the FDA about a “potential path forward for further clinical development of intranasal foralumab in na-SPMS,” according to the release.
Foralumab is Tiziana’s lead candidate, with ongoing mid-phase testing of the asset in multiple system atrophy, Alzheimer’s disease and ALS. The investigational immunotherapy is also being assessed in an open-label extension program for na-SPMS.
The biotech’s only other publicly listed asset is an anti-IL-6 receptor monoclonal antibody called TZLS-501. In December 2025, on the back of increasing industry interest in IL-6, Tiziana said it would spin out TZLS-501 into a separate publicly traded company to boost the strategic focus of each company. Since then, there’s been no update on the planned spinout.

The Lectric XP series has become something of an institution in the American electric bicycle market. As the country’s best-selling e-bike lineup, it’s helped put hundreds of thousands of riders on two wheels, largely thanks to its combination of affordable pricing, impressive performance, and practical features. It’s become the go-to electric bike in the US, but that hasn’t made Lectric complacent. Instead, the company is continuing to innovate.
Now, Lectric is giving its flagship XP4 a fresh makeover with three new limited-edition versions, each sporting a unique color and a new collection of accessories and upgrades designed for different types of riders, from urban assault roles to conquering your favorite off-road fishing spots.
The new Lectric XP4 Limited Editions come in three flavors: District, (black) Jubilee (pink), and Ridge (green). Each is priced at $1,399 and includes a 750W motor, upgraded accessories, and a distinctive matte paint job. That’s just a $100 premium over the existing XP 750, yet comes with a whole new host of accessories designed specifically for each special edition model.

source_document.body:
U.S. Steel broke ground on a $1.9 billion iron production plant in Osceola, Arkansas, to supply its nearby steel mill. The project will connect the company’s Minnesota iron ore mines with steel production at its Big River Steel Works campus.
What’s Related
The facility is expected to create about 200 full-time jobs and roughly 2,000 construction jobs at peak. Preliminary site preparation is underway, and construction is expected to start later this year.
The plant will produce direct reduced iron (DRI), made by removing oxygen from iron ore without melting it. It will supply Big River 2’s electric arc furnaces, which use electricity to melt scrap and iron into steel. The steel will go to customers in the automotive , appliance and solar industries.
The October announcement did not give a production start date. In May, company officials told the Association for Iron & Steel Technology that they expected the facility to come online in the first half of 2029.
RELATED: U.S. Steel Invests $475M to Expand Alabama Pipe Production
More control over raw materials
The project will use iron ore pellets from U.S. Steel’s Keetac mine in Minnesota. The company will turn its own ore into DRI for its Arkansas furnaces. U.S. Steel says DRI can replace high-quality scrap used in steelmaking, helping the company manage costs and secure a more reliable supply.
“From a rock in the ground to a coil from our mill, this facility creates a true mine-to-mill connection within U. S. Steel,” said Daniel Brown, executive vice president of advanced technology steelmaking and chief operating officer of Big River Steel Works. “It gives us greater control over a critical raw material, strengthens supply reliability and provides more flexibility to produce the advanced steels our customers need.”
Feeding hot iron directly into the mill
The new plant will sit next to Big River 2, allowing iron to enter the furnaces while still hot. U.S. Steel has said that this arrangement improves efficiency and reduces electricity needs.
The facility will also compress the iron into solid pieces called hot briquetted iron. That form is easier to transport and can be used elsewhere on the Big River campus or shipped to other sites.
Another investment at Big River
U.S. Steel announced the iron plant investment in April. Parent company Nippon Steel said the project is part of its $11 billion investment commitment.
The project follows the $3 billion Big River 2 expansion , which began producing steel in 2024. U.S. Steel acquired Big River Steel in 2021, and the combined campus now has four electric arc furnaces and produces more than 6 million tons of steel annually.

source_document.body:
Lime buildup coats pipes and valves in a neglected lime system. Credit: Carmeuse Systems
By: Northern Miner Staff November 2, 2026
Poorly maintained lime systems can raise costs, disrupt pH control and force processing plants to shut down, says Darren Farnworth, lime systems specialist at Carmeuse Systems.
In an interview with The Northern Miner’s Devan Murugan, Farnworth explains how copper and gold operations can spot problems early, improve maintenance and prevent lime preparation from becoming a production bottleneck.
The Northern Miner: Why is lime important to copper and gold production, and why is it often overlooked?
Darren Farnworth: Lime is used for pH control principally, and it tends to be one of those background processes that people just expect to be there. How you use lime and how you make it has a huge effect on how stable your process can be. Ultimately, that means you’re going to get better production and more uptime and run a more stable facility.
TNM: What’s the most common misconception about lime systems in non-ferrous mining?
DF: Probably the most common misconception is that all lime is the same.
While the chemical is essentially the same, how it is produced, or how it’s made when you make down that lime at your facility, has a really direct impact on how stable your process can be, how reactive that lime will be and how useful it will be in making gold and copper.
TNM: What patterns do you see at facilities that consistently struggle with their lime systems?
Watch the full interview above.
DF: Probably the most common pattern is that it gets ignored. It is often in its own little room, it’s enclosed, and it’s left to its own devices. If it is working, that’s fantastic. If something breaks, they close the door and hope the night shift can fix it.
When lime is overlooked, it increases your maintenance costs, it can increase your downtime, and it can affect the stability of your process as it goes through.
The other thing is that not all lime slurry is the same. Once it’s made, it looks the same. It looks like a white milk of lime, but how it is made directly affects how reactive and useful that product can be to the production downstream.
TNM: What are the early warning signs that a system isn’t performing as it should?
DF: Probably the most common one is a lot of manual interruptions or manual adjustments.
If your lime system is not running in automatic and you have maintenance people or operations bypassing things, running around the automatic controls, that’s a very good sign.
You could see consumption increases that aren’t tied to production increases. You’re seeing more lime consumed than you normally would.
You pretty regularly will see scale buildup and a big mess around lime systems that have been neglected. Ultimately, you’re doing repetitive maintenance. You’re doing the same thing over and over again, particularly if it’s unplanned.
TNM: What happens if those warning signs are ignored?
DF: The smallest impact will be a loss of stability. Plants will find that they’re having a hard time maintaining their pH control, and they wind up chasing that problem downstream.
You will consume more lime, so you’ve got higher lime costs. Your maintenance costs can go up, and not just cost, but mental energy.
People are committing time and energy to focusing on their lime system when they could otherwise be spending that on overall production.
The worst-case scenario is downtime. If the whole plant has to shut down because you can’t maintain your pH balance, that has a huge impact.
TNM: Can you give an example of a seemingly minor problem that affected overall plant performance?
DF: One of my colleagues on the raw materials side of the business had noticed that a customer had started ordering super sacks of lime in addition to their regular bulk shipments.
We made a trip out there to figure out what was going on. What was happening was that they were slaking so poorly, their reaction was so poorly controlled, that they were unable to meet their production needs, meet their pH targets, and were having to put this manual intervention in place.
In reality, their system should have been able to fully meet their requirements, plus some additional capacity for an expansion that they’re planning.
But because they had let their lime system sort of fall out of service gradually over time, they weren’t able to meet their production targets.
TNM: What do operations with well-run lime systems do differently?
DF: The first thing I notice when I find myself at a facility that is running well is that it’s clean.
Cleaning up the lime system allows them to see when things are going wrong and identify problems quickly and early.
Those operations also really understand why lime matters to their process. They monitor the performance, not just of their overall production, but in terms of some key metrics of their lime system, be that density, lime consumption or the overall availability of the system.
Rather than just ignore it, they dig into root causes.
Probably the most important factor that those operations have is that they have a continuous improvement attitude. If they see something, they fix something. They’re always looking to improve it.
They’re training their operators in between so that there are more people who have knowledge within their organization, so that it doesn’t rely on a single individual being responsible for that operation.
TNM: How important are lime systems as producers try to increase output from existing plants?
DF: They’re trying to do more with less. They’re trying to increase production at existing facilities and really maximize that output because building new facilities is so much more expensive and difficult.
Keeping that system easy to operate and running on automatic allows them then to focus their energy on the other bottlenecks in their plants.
The last thing we want is the lime system to be a bottleneck.
TNM: If an operator suspects a problem, where should they start?
DF: Start grabbing some data. That’s always a useful thing in any diagnostic.
Track your volume consumption. Track how it moves up and down as your production moves up and down. Take some quality measurements. Keep track of how much maintenance you’re doing on a given system.
Then there’s a matter of starting to look for ways to improve.
There are outside views. It’s folks like us that can come in and look at your system, and we have observations that we see because we look at these every day.
But you can also find that training internally. Bring people in from either other operations within your organization or even completely different systems.
It’s amazing what a fresh set of eyes can do to really understand what is working and not working.

Electric trucks made up 50.3% of all heavy trucks sold in China in September. That’s 33,100 electric big rigs in a single month, up 37% from a year ago, while the overall heavy-truck market shrank by 21%.
And it’s showing up in the oil data. China’s diesel demand is on track to fall by about 230,000 barrels per day this year, and trucks running on batteries and natural gas are doing most of the work.
From 14% to half in under two years
In 2024, new-energy vehicles accounted for 13.6% of heavy trucks (12 tonnes and up) sold in China. In 2025, sales nearly tripled to 231,100 units, up 182%, for a 28.9% share.
Electric heavy trucks passed 50% of China’s sales in September 2026.
December 2025 hit 53.9%, but that was a rush. Buyers piled in before trade-in subsidies expired and new purchase tax costs kicked in, and the share dropped back to about 23% by March.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Then it came right back. Through the first nine months of 2026, China sold 226,400 electric heavy trucks, up 64%, for a 38.1% share. That’s already almost as many as in all of 2025, with a quarter still to go. In tractors, the big rigs that pull long-haul trailers, the September share hit 64.5%.
China sold almost as many electric heavy trucks in nine months of 2026 as in all of 2025.
That’s well ahead of Beijing’s own plan. This year, 11 government bodies set a target of 40% new-energy heavy-truck sales by 2030, along with 1.6 million of them on the road, 30,000 km of zero-carbon freight corridors and about 3,000 charging and swap stations. The market blew past that sales target four years early on a monthly basis, and CATL now says new-energy trucks will be half of China’s annual truck sales by 2028.
Why Chinese fleets are switching
It comes down to cost. In most uses, an electric heavy truck in China is now cheaper to own and run than a diesel one, and fleets run that math every day.
CATL claims savings of about 0.6 yuan per km. Independent numbers are more measured, but still favorable: a study by the ICCT and China’s CATARC found battery-electric trucks about 19% cheaper per tonne-km than diesel in good conditions, though they lose that edge at low annual mileage or when battery weight eats into payload.
Charging time is the other objection, and China’s answer is swapping. CATL’s Qiji brand operated about 300 heavy-truck swap stations at the end of 2025 and plans 900 by the end of this year and 2,000 in 2027. In August, it agreed to pay 2.56 billion yuan (about $370 million) for nearly 25% of Qiyuan Green Power, China’s largest heavy-truck swap operator with more than 1,600 charging and swap stations. Its new standardized packs hold 432 kWh and 513 kWh and swap in about five minutes.
CATL is already taking the swapping model to Europe with Octopus Energy .
The trucks themselves are domestic. XCMG led the segment in 2025 with a 15.4% share, ahead of SANY and FAW Jiefang, and the top three held 42.9% of the market. CATL supplied 60% of the batteries.
Electric is eating LNG, too
For years, the alternative to diesel trucks in China was liquefied natural gas. LNG trucks took nearly 30% of the market in 2024, when gas was much cheaper than diesel.
Now they’re losing to batteries. According to Kpler, LNG trucks had a 37% share of heavy-duty registrations in March, against 23% for electric. By July, electric was at 47% and LNG had collapsed to 11%. Monthly LNG truck registrations fell from more than 30,000 to about 6,200.
Electric trucks overtook LNG trucks in China’s heavy-duty registrations in 2026.
So China is skipping the “bridge fuel” phase for trucks almost as fast as it started it.
Diesel demand is falling
China’s diesel consumption already peaked. Rhodium Group found that diesel refinery runs topped out in April 2023, and apparent consumption dropped from 4.7 million barrels per day then to 4.0 million barrels per day in April 2025.
2026 is the steepest drop yet. Kpler estimates diesel demand fell about 420,000 barrels per day year-over-year in May, roughly 10%, and 460,000 in June. It expects a decline of about 230,000 barrels per day for the full year and only a 64,000 barrel-per-day rebound in 2027.
LNG and electric trucks displaced about 680,000 barrels per day of diesel in China in 2026, according to Kpler.
Kpler puts the gross diesel displacement from alternative trucks at about 680,000 barrels per day this year: roughly 450,000 from the LNG fleet built in recent years and 230,000 from electric trucks. Road freight still grew about 3% through July. China is moving more goods with less diesel.
There’s a catch. The fuel price spike this spring, tied to the Iran war, cut demand on its own and pushed more fleets toward electric. But that only explains part of it, and the fleet is still early: electric trucks will be only about 8% of China’s heavy trucks on the road by the end of 2026, according to Kpler. Every year of 40-50% sales shares compounds the diesel losses.
Meanwhile in Europe and the US
Europe is growing fast from a tiny base. ACEA data shows 5,120 heavy electric trucks (16 tonnes and up) registered in the EU through September, up 59.9%, for a 2.5% share. That’s up from 1.7% a year ago, but diesel still took 91.7% of all EU truck registrations.
A few countries stand out. Switzerland is at 24%, Norway 14.4%, the Netherlands 11.1% and Sweden 10.3%. Germany registered the most units at 1,722, but that’s only a 4.2% share.
The US doesn’t publish an official electric Class 8 sales figure, and that tells you something. The best indicator is the recent order for 2,500 Tesla Semis through ZET SCALE , which would roughly double the number of electric Class 8 trucks on US roads. Against about 230,000 Class 8 trucks sold per year, the electric share is well under 1%.
China’s electric share of heavy-truck sales is more than 15 times Europe’s.
Price is the big difference. The ICCT puts the median electric Class 8 tractor in the US at $411,200, against $172,500 for diesel. Federal tax credits for commercial EVs ended in 2025, and California shelved the rule that would have required fleets to buy zero-emission trucks.
Electrek’s Take
This is the biggest under-covered story in the EV industry right now.
Everyone argued for years about whether electric semis could work. Range, weight, charging, cost. China settled it the boring way. It got the price of a battery-electric heavy truck close enough to diesel, built swap stations along freight routes, and let fleet operators do what fleet operators always do: pick the cheapest truck per kilometer.
And the result is showing up where it matters, in oil demand. Trucks are where diesel lives. Displacing a quarter of a million barrels a day in one year, with electric trucks still only around 8% of the fleet, means we’re still early on this curve.
The contrast with the US is hard to watch. America has Tesla, a Semi factory in Nevada built for 50,000 trucks a year, and some of the best freight corridors in the world for electrification. But electric Class 8 trucks cost 2.4 times as much as diesel here, the federal incentives are gone, and the market is under 1%. The ZET SCALE order is real progress. But it came from shippers pooling their demand, and twe have yet to see these trucks get delivered.

A partial view of the Wona underground operation. Credit: Endeavour Mining.
Posted By: FREDERIC TOMESCO November 2, 2026
Endeavour Mining (TSX, LSE: EDV) suspended underground mining at its Mana gold mine in Burkina Faso after part of an access road sank, adding another setback at an operation already expected to miss its annual production target.
The Oct. 28 incident restricted access to two underground entrances, Dangouna and Aviera, through the depleted Wona open pit, Endeavour said Monday . Workers were evacuated, nobody was injured and local authorities were notified. Mining has been stopped at all three active underground entrances while specialists assess ground stability and repairs.
Endeavour didn’t immediately disclose the cause of the incident or announce a restart date.
Despite the incident, Endeavour said it remains on track to hit full-year production and all-in sustaining cost targets even if no further mining occurs at Mana in the fourth quarter. Endeavour previously said it expected 2026 output to range between 1.09 million oz. and 1.27 million ounces.
“The overall impact will depend on how long portal remediation takes (we think one to two quarters) and on whether open pit feed, subject to permitting, can supplement throughput,” National Bank Financial mining analyst Mohamed Sidibé said Monday in a note.
Repair plan
Endeavour is considering restarting and accelerating mining through the Wona entrance, which remains accessible, and drawing on nearby open pits to limit lost production. It plans to outline the ground assessment and repair plan when it reports third-quarter results on Nov. 12.
The disruption follows an earlier ground-stability concern. In July, Endeavour disclosed that mining at Aviera had paused that month to monitor a surface fracture in the depleted Wona pit above the deposit. At the time, it said the fracture didn’t affect active ore zones and anticipated resuming work around mid-third quarter, subject to monitoring.
Monday’s announcement didn’t say whether that fracture and the latest subsidence were connected.
The event disclosed Monday “appears to have occurred on a structure parallel to the July one, though it is too early to tell if they are related,” Sidibé said. Mana represents about 5% of the company’s net asset value, according to his calculations.
Along with the Houndé mine, Mana is one of Endeavour’s two producing assets in Burkina Faso. In West Africa, the company also produces gold in Côte d’Ivoire and Senegal.
Earlier depletion
Mana’s difficulties also extend beyond ground conditions. Endeavour warned in July that annual output would fall below the bottom of its original 155,000–180,000 oz. target, with sustaining costs exceeding guidance. It attributed the weakness partly to earlier depletion of the higher-grade Siou underground deposit after unsuccessful drilling to extend its resources, and delayed mining at the Bana Camp open pit.
First-half production fell to 68,000 oz. from 87,000 oz. a year earlier, a decline of about 22%. Mana accounted for about 12% of Endeavour’s first-half output.
London-based Endeavour owns 85% of Mana, with Burkina Faso’s government holding the balance. The mine lies about 60 km north of Houndé.
Mana’s processing plant began operating in 2008, and the mine shifted to fully underground production in 2024. It produced 173,000 oz. last year.
Endeavour’s longer-term strategy is to extend its operating life beyond a decade by expanding underground deposits and evaluating nearby surface targets. Restoring reliable access to those underground workings is now the immediate priority for the operation.Top of FormBottom of Form
Toronto-traded shares of Endeavour rose 0.9% to C$70.33 Monday morning, valuing the company at about C$17 billion ($12.2 billion). The stock has traded between C$53.37 and C$98.71 in the past year.

Boeing will convert a 767-300 passenger jet into a freighter for Icelease, which also took options for up to two more conversions, as the leasing company continues to grow its freighter portfolio, the companies announced on Monday.
The first aircraft is scheduled to take its production slot in the first quarter of 2027, with delivery of the converted aircraft expected in the second quarter. Boeing ( NYSE: B A) said it will convert the airplanes at partner ST Engineering’s airframe overhaul facilities in Singapore.
Icelease was formed 20 years ago as the leasing arm of Icelandair. It owns, or will purchase the 767s and will deliver them to ST Engineering for the retrofit work.
“This agreement with Boeing to convert up to three Boeing 767 aircraft marks an important milestone for both Icelease and its Dublin-based sister company IAT Leasing,” said Sigthor Einarsson, managing partner, Icelease. “The Boeing 767-300 converted freighter will join the growing managed cargo aircraft portfolio of IAT Leasing, which already includes seven Boeing 737-800BCF and other freighters leased to various customers.”
Some of those B737-800 converted freighters are currently on lease to ASL Aviation Holdings, which operates several airlines in Europe and Australia supporting express carriers, and Tianjin Air Cargo in China.
The 767-300 is the world’s most popular medium widebody converted freighter and has a range of 3,3000 nautical miles with a 57 metric ton-payload.
Global demand for widebody freighters is high as cargo volumes continue to grow, wars force airlines to make long detours and use more aircraft to meet customer needs and many large freighters are retired. The feedstock of passenger 767s available for conversion is dwindling and carriers are slowly turning to the Airbus A330-300 converted freighter to meet future replacement and growth requirements.

Sail Biomedicine’s $925 million deal with Johnson & Johnson helped boost the cell and gene therapy sector over biologics in terms of venture capital fundraising in the third quarter.
The cell therapy space has been rocked by recent reports of deaths in clinical trials being run by Novartis and Bristol Myers Squibb. And yet, cell and gene therapy brought home the second most venture capital dollars in the third quarter, outpacing biologics, according to PitchBook.
Cell and gene therapy took in $2.2 billion in venture capital in the third period across 51 deals, falling behind small molecules at $3.2 billion but ahead of biologics, which amassed $1.5 billion.
This is only the second time since 2022 that cell and gene therapy (CGT) has beaten biologics in terms of fundraising, PitchBook said, and results from both are a jump in CGT funding and a significant drop in biologics over second quarter totals.
The achievement comes as the cell therapy sector has been rocked by reports of multiple deaths in autoimmune trials at some of the biggest pharmas in the space, PitchBook pointed out. In late August, news broke that Novartis had paused a handful of clinical trials for the CAR T rapcabtagene autoleucel after three deaths . Then last month, Bristol Myers Squibb reported a death in a multiple sclerosis trial for its CAR T zolacabtagene autoleucel (zola-cel), after having previously paused certain zola-cel trials to investigate some safety signals. The deaths occurred months prior to the news breaking but were confirmed by the pharmas more recently.
Meanwhile, CAR T biotech Caribou Biosciences announced the suspension of R&D activities amid what CEO Rachel Haurwitz called a challenging fundraising environment for allogeneic cell therapy. The biotech was co-founded by Nobel Prize-winning CRISPR pioneer Jennifer Doudna but ran into myriad troubles as the cell therapy space shifted from cancer to autoimmune thanks to groundbreaking research in lupus that came out in 2023.

Weighing the risks of CAR T in autoimmune disease as Kyverna nears market
Not a month after reports of three deaths in autoimmune trials for Novartis’ CAR T cell therapy ignited a debate about the use of these treatments in nonfatal diseases, Kyverna Therapeutics reported data bolstering its case to bring to market the first CAR T for an autoimmune disease.

These events would lead an observer to think that cell therapy—particularly for less lethal conditions like autoimmune—was on the outs. But PitchBook’s analysis shows a more hopeful look at the space, as does Kyverna Therapeutics’ advancement toward an FDA application for the CAR T mivocabtagene autoleucel (miv-cel) in stiff person syndrome .
Leading the Q3 fundraising was Sail Biomedicines, which secured a massive deal with Johnson & Johnson worth up to $925 million initially, including an equity purchase. PitchBook flagged the fundraising event as venture capital given the involvement of J&J’s JJDC venture arm. Upfront payments totaled $785 million, including a $465 million equity investment. An additional $140 million in development-based milestones were offered on the back end. But the healthcare giant also secured an exclusive option to purchase Sail later on for $2.58 billion.
The deal, which closed in August, gave the biotech a valuation of $2.8 billion, according to Pitchbook. Unlike Caribou’s allogenic CAR T approach, Sail is advancing in vivo CAR T therapies for immune-mediated conditions. J&J expects assets from that collaboration to hit the clinic this year, according to a company presentation at the Morgan Stanley 24th Annual Global Healthcare Conference in September.
That J&J would make such a play for a cell therapy company is not a surprise. The Big Pharma is one of the leaders in the space with Legend Biotech–partnered blood cancer therapy Cavykti .
PitchBook also highlighted seed rounds from K2 Therapeutics for $50 million and Cirrus Therapeutics’ $14.7 million as key cell and gene therapy investments in the quarter.
Pediatric-focused cell therapy company BrainChild Bio had the second highest series A in the period with $116 million, behind Solstice Oncology’s $225 million. Link Cell Therapies raised $90 million in the quarter.
Cell therapy has continued to make news in the fourth quarter as well, with former J&J executive Paul Stoffels rescuing a clutch of assets from his former biotech Galapagos to form Armed Cell Therapeutics. The biotech broke cover in mid-October after striking a deal with Lakefront Biotherapeutics—formerly Galapagos—to take over the assets for just under $240 million in biobucks.

Bioscience employment rose in 41 states, though not in California, according to a new report from the Biotechnology Innovation Organization and the Council of State Bioscience Associations.
The U.S. bioscience industry experienced employment and business establishment growth from 2021 to 2025, according to a new report from the Biotechnology Innovation Organization (BIO) and the Council of State Bioscience Associations (CSBA). The industry directly employed 2.31 million people across more than 156,000 businesses last year, representing 7% and 22% jumps, respectively, from 2021.
Employment increased in 41 states, plus the District of Columbia and Puerto Rico . Absolute job growth leaders were Texas , Florida , Massachusetts , Illinois , North Carolina , Pennsylvania , New York , Ohio and New Jersey .
Data were mixed when comparing Massachusetts and the nation’s largest bioscience employer, California . In Massachusetts, employment rose 10% from 2021 to 2025, reaching 145,864 industry jobs across 5,934 business establishments last year. However, California had a 1.5% employment decline, with 334,448 jobs across 15,719 businesses in 2025.
Among the highlights for Massachusetts:
Research, testing and medical laboratories, the state’s largest bioscience subsector, grew by 14.6% from 2021 to 2025, surpassing the 8.1% increase for the nation.
Pharmaceuticals employment increased 9.7% from 2021 to 2025, outpacing the 5.4% change in the U.S.
Annual bioscience wages averaged $219,393 last year, 115% higher than Massachusetts’ private-sector average of $101,877.
Despite California’s employment decline, there was positive news for the state.
Research, testing and medical laboratories, the state’s largest bioscience subsector, grew 2.5%.
California’s overall bioscience employment concentration was 25% higher than the national average.
Annual bioscience wages averaged $185,005 last year, 90% higher than the state’s private-sector average of $97,184.
Research, testing and medical labs was not only California and Massachusetts’ largest bioscience subsector but the nation’s as well. It employed more than 779,000 people in the U.S. in 2025, which represented about one-third of the country’s bioscience employment. From 2021 to 2025, the subsector’s jobs grew 8.1% and its establishments 37%.
While highlighting the report’s positive data, BIO President and CEO John Crowley said in a press release that the U.S. must continue promoting an environment that supports scientific discovery and strengthens the country’s leadership in biotechnology.
“This report makes clear that we cannot take that strength for granted,” he said. “Now is the time to invest in America’s biotech ecosystem, advance policies that foster innovation and lay the groundwork for America’s long-term leadership for years to come. The public policies enacted today at the national and state level will directly impact whether American biotech continues to thrive here at home and where the next generation of breakthroughs will be developed.”

Police arrested a 78-year-old Philadelphia woman last month after she blocked a delivery robot on a sidewalk, an act she described as a protest against the machines’ use of public space.
What’s Related
Carolyn Marvin , a retired University of Pennsylvania communications professor, received a disorderly conduct citation. Police said she refused repeated orders to move out of the robot’s path, according to reports by CNN and Philadelphia television station WPVI.
Marvin told CNN she had stopped in front of delivery robots before, sometimes delaying them for 10 or 15 minutes. This was the first time she had been arrested for doing so.
“I was under the impression that I had more rights than the robot did,” Marvin explained. She said her objections include potential job losses for delivery workers, sidewalk safety , and privacy concerns involving the robots’ cameras.
A peaceful protest
Police told WPVI that witnesses called to report a disturbance involving Marvin and an Uber delivery robot. Officers said she ignored their commands to let it pass.
Marvin described her actions as peaceful protest and said she believes they are protected free speech. She told WPVI: “I have been protesting them whenever I saw them by standing in front of them and preventing them from going forward.”
Uber Eats introduced robot deliveries in Philadelphia in March. CNN reported that the company did not respond to its request for comment.
Pennsylvania’s rules for delivery robots
Pennsylvania passed a law in 2020 that added personal delivery devices to its definition of pedestrians. The law covers ground-based machines that transport goods using remote control, autonomous driving, or both.
The law also places requirements on the machines. In pedestrian areas, they must yield to people walking and cyclists or safely navigate around them. Their speed is limited to 12 mph in those areas.
Marvin plans to contest the disorderly conduct charge on First Amendment grounds, The Daily Pennsylvanian reported. At Penn, she taught a course called “History and Theory of Freedom of Expression.”

1956 Chrysler New Yorker Parked for Decades Is a Rare St. Regis, a Sad Sight
10 photos
Photo: Bobs Classic Cars & Parts/YouTube
Introduced in 1940, the Chrysler New Yorker remained in continuous production through 1996 (minus the WW2 years). It served as the brand's flagship model, and it's Chrysler's longest-running nameplate . It also spawned a few cool limited-edition vehicles, including the St. Regis.
The most recent Mopar to sport the St. Regis badge was actually a Dodge. The full-size car was offered between 1979 and 1981. However, it also graced the New Yorker on two occasions. Chrysler sold one between 1974 and 1978, while the original version hit dealerships in 1955 and 1956.
The St. Regis arrived on the fourth-generation New Yorker, which was a significant departure from its predecessor. The 1955 luxury car had its design based on the custom 1952 Imperial Parade Phaeton limo, which was penned by Virgil Exner. The styling kicked off the Forward Look era, lasting through 1961.
The St. Regis badge was reserved for two-door hardtop models with exclusive two-tone paint. The options list also included a choice of three-tone paint schemes. The bundle also included a bit of extra chrome trim, a textured vinyl headliner, cloth upholstery inserts, and a color-keyed cabin. The St. Regis did nothing for the New Yorker in the performance department.
The model was somewhat popular for a luxury vehicle in 1955. Of the 52,178 New Yorkers delivered, exactly 11,076 had St. Regis badges. That's a little over 21% of the total output. In 1956, New Yorker deliveries dropped to 41,140 examples, with the St. Regis model finding 6,686 homes (16% of the total production).
Although it's not rare by production numbers, the original New Yorker St. Regis is a pretty rare sight nowadays. And that's because most of them are rotting away in junkyards and backyards, much like the 1956 hardtop you see here.
Spotted at an estate sale, this St. Regis rolled off the assembly line in a three-tone finish . But it's no longer a pretty sight. Parked for decades and picked for parts, the Mopar is a sad sight. The car is missing its trunk lid and the passenger door, as well as much of the interior. Unfortunately, the original drivetrain was also removed.
But we can still see that it rolled off the assembly line in a three-tone finish. It was a black roof, while the rest of the body is a white-on-red combo. I bet that this St. Regis was a gorgeous sight when it was new.
Is it worth restoring? Well, not really. A rotisserie restoration could cost up to six figures nowadays, and these Mopars don't fetch nearly as much in perfect condition at public auctions. I've seen only a couple go for over $40,000, and a few others reached into $30,000 territory. As far as I know, no St. Regis fetched beyond $50,000 (though the rarest New Yorker convertibles did on a few occasions).
Does this hardtop have a future in any form, or should it be parted out and sent to the crusher ? Check it out in the video below and tell me your thoughts in the comments section.

Posted By: Colin McClelland November 2, 2026
Ontario has added Mayfair Gold’s (TSXV: MFG; NYSE-A: MINE) Fenn-Gib gold project to its accelerated permitting program, making the proposed development near Timmins the fourth selected under the province’s One Project, One Process framework .
The designation puts provincial approvals and Indigenous consultation under a coordinated review led by the Ministry of Energy and Mines. Mayfair is targeting a construction start in 2028 and first production in 2030, while Ontario estimates the project would support 450 construction jobs and 250 long-term positions.
“For too long, permitting delays stood in the way of getting Ontario’s resources to market,” Energy and Mines Minister Stephen Lecce said in a statement Monday. “To compete, we must be the best, which is why our government is planning to further accelerate permitting this fall, to get mines built faster, unlocking billions in investment to create more good-paying jobs right here at home.”
The decision advances Mayfair’s effort to develop a smaller, higher-grade starter operation within Fenn-Gib’s much larger gold resource. It also adds another gold development to a provincial program initially launched with lithium and nickel projects, as Ontario seeks to demonstrate that coordinating reviews can translate into construction.
Financing takes shape
Mayfair lined up financing of up to $310 million (US$218 million) from Australia’s Macquarie Bank in October. The proposed package comprises a $300-million project loan and a $10-million equity investment, compared with Fenn-Gib’s estimated $450-million initial development cost.
Macquarie completed the investment on Oct. 14, buying about 2.35 million shares at $4.26 apiece. The proposed debt financing remains subject to due diligence, definitive agreements and closing conditions, Mayfair said.
The loan proposal includes an early $25-million drawdown to support work ahead of full construction financing, including engineering, equipment orders and preliminary construction activities. The proposed debt would cover about two-thirds of initial capital costs, leaving Mayfair to arrange the balance.
Fenn-Gib, about 80 km east of Timmins, hosts 181.3 million indicated tonnes grading 0.74 gram gold per tonne for 4.3 million oz. contained metal, and 8.9 million inferred tonnes at 0.49 gram for 141,000 oz., according to its September 2024 resource estimate.
January’s prefeasibility study focused on probable reserves of 25.1 million tonnes grading 1.29 grams gold per tonne for about 1 million oz. contained metal. The development plan envisages processing 4,800 tonnes daily over a 14.3-year operating life, producing an average of about 64,100 oz. annually, including 71,300 oz. a year during the first six years.
Coordinated reviews
Fenn-Gib joins Frontier Lithium’s (TSXV: FL; US-OTC: LITOF) PAK lithium project, Canada Nickel’s (TSXV: CNC; US-OTC: CNIKF) Crawford nickel project and Kinross Gold’s (TSX: K; NYSE: KGC) Great Bear gold project under the framework, launched in October 2025.
Ontario aims to halve government review times by giving developers a single provincial contact to coordinate approvals across ministries. The designation does not itself grant the permits needed for construction, and the Crown’s duty to consult Indigenous communities remains in place, the province said.
Lecce previously told TNM that Ontario was targeting permitting timelines of about two years. He later outlined plans to extend the reforms to early exploration, advanced exploration and expansions at operating mines.
Mayfair shares finished Friday at $3.10 in Toronto, 6.6% weaker on the day, ahead of Monday’s announcement.
“The One Project, One Process designation is an important milestone for the Fenn-Gib Gold Project and reinforces Ontario’s commitment to responsible, investment-ready mining development,” Mayfair CEO Drew Anwyll said in the provincial statement.
“This framework provides greater coordination and predictability as we advance Fenn-Gib through permitting and development, helping move the project closer to construction and the significant employment and economic opportunities it can create for the region.”
