Spain's former foreign minister Ana Palacio urges strong EU support for mining to mirror American policy. Credit: The Northern Miner.
Posted By: Colin McClelland November 2, 2026
One of the clearest arguments for learning from U.S. President Donald Trump’s mining policy came recently from a former Spanish foreign minister in Seville . Ana Palacio urged Europe to study Washington’s tax credits and purchase guarantees. Governments that want strategic mineral production, she argued, must help make it commercially possible.
Canada might want to listen. It should also distinguish the useful part of the American approach from the uncertainty that accompanies it. Sharing investment risk can help build a mine. Trade disputes make governments and once-trusted allies harder to rely on.
That tension runs through Trump’s mining policy. His administration deserves credit for recognizing that supply security costs money. The question is whether its interventions will create an enduring industrial base, and whether partners can depend on the rules governing their participation.
Washington’s deal with MP Materials illustrates the opportunity. Announced in July 2025, the Pentagon agreement established a 10-year floor of $110 per kg for the company’s neodymium-praseodymium products and purchase assurances for magnets from a planned factory. Those commitments address revenue risk, something a faster permit alone cannot fix.
Transparency
There is a legitimate public interest in paying for supply capacity that markets might otherwise leave concentrated elsewhere. But public support needs transparent terms, measurable obligations and a return for taxpayers. Strategic importance cannot become an exemption from commercial scrutiny.
Nor does domestic support cancel the damage of unpredictable trade policy. Washington exempted critical minerals from its July tariffs on Canadian goods, but separate duties on steel, aluminum and copper products show the limits of that protection. The wider message to investors is that access to an allied market can become a bargaining instrument in disputes far removed from a deposit’s economics.
Spain offers a useful comparison, though hardly a finished model. At the Mining and Minerals Hall conference in October, the recurring demand was for rules and investment commitments that last long enough to carry a project into production.
“Mining needs stability,” Palacio said. “We need big pacts, big agreements where everybody commits.”
Developers in Seville described trying to coordinate financing, equipment orders and recruitment while approval schedules remain uncertain. Spain’s proposed national exploration program envisages €197 million (C$311.5 million) in public and private investment, but public funding depends on annual appropriations. Better geological information will help; companies still need to know when they can use it.
In Andalusia, regional industry minister Jorge Paradela pointed to Atalaya Mining’s processing technology, the Cobre Las Cruces redevelopment and Atlantic Copper’s recycling project as ways to retain more value locally. The region already accounts for 90% of Spain’s metal mining value.
That industrial ambition is worth borrowing, as is the recognition that Europe cannot supply everything itself. Andalusia’s mining director general, Jesús Portillo García-Pintos, argued for stronger domestic capabilities connected through reliable international supply chains. Canada has every reason to help build those connections, and consulate staff were trying to make it happen in Seville.
Special label
But neither Spain nor Canada can sell certainty just by declaring projects strategic. Atalaya’s Touro project in Galicia remains in permitting after receiving that status in 2024. A special label is useful only if it changes the administrative work, funding or infrastructure needed to reach a decision.
Ottawa has a $2-billion Critical Minerals Sovereign Fund intended to support projects through investments and purchase agreements. The First and Last Mile Fund offers up to $1.5 billion through 2030 for mining and infrastructure. These are commitments to judge by deployment and results, not announcement totals.
Canada’s next task is to connect those tools to buyers, power, transport and credible approval schedules. Trade diversification should produce contracts with European and other customers, backed by the processing capacity and logistics needed to deliver.
Durability also requires public confidence in Canada and the U.S. Faster decisions should come from properly staffed regulators, coordinated reviews and clear requirements. Weakening environmental scrutiny risks litigation and distrust that can outlast any time saved. Indigenous participation and tangible benefits for neighbouring communities belong in project development from the outset.
Washington has already shown that some mining commitments can survive a change of government. The Pentagon funded processing work at MP Materials during Trump’s first term and again under President Joe Biden, before Trump’s much larger agreement last year. The company has benefited from successive administrations pursuing the same industrial objective.
A mine that takes a decade to develop cannot depend on a four-year political horizon. Agreements should survive elections because their purpose is clear and their obligations are enforceable, whoever holds ministerial office.
As Americans approach the midterm elections, Canada should resist treating mining policy as a choice between Trump’s interventionism and European caution. We need governments willing to shoulder defined risks, capable of making timely decisions and reliable enough to keep agreements. The most useful promise a government can make to a mine is one its successor will honour.

WASHINGTON — The Pentagon has shipped some cyber operators from Maryland to sunny Hawaii in an effort to reinforce US Pacific Command’s technical defenses there under a concept called Cyber Defense Forces Pacific, according to a senior PACOM official.
Brig. Gen. Michael Smith, director for command, control, communications, computers and cyber at PACOM, told the TechNet Indo-Pacific Conference that the newcomers assigned to the Defense Information Systems Agency Pacific provide “a level of additional cybersecurity defense here in this theater.” DISA-Pacific is the regional field command of the Fort Meade-based organization.
“[I’m] really thankful for those folks because when they weren’t here, it’s just me,” he said at the event last week.
The personnel were drawn from the DoD’s Cyber Defense Command (DCDC), which is also based in Fort Meade in Maryland. The DCDC falls under US Cyber Command and is responsible for defending the Pentagon’s data networks.
Smith called the relocation to Hawaii of some servicemembers a “roll down” of DCDC personnel to PACOM’s area of responsibility, meant to “build out a more robust defender perspective with all the tools and assets to go with that.” The newly assigned personnel are trained to be adept at protecting information and responding to incidents, he said.
While Smith did not discuss any specific threats to PACOM networks, the command operates in the region with perhaps America’s most technically proficient adversary: China. Experts say that Beijing, for instance, has been caught targeting the networks of military critical infrastructure installations in Guam , a key US military installation, in an effort to cripple a Washington response to action in the region.
In the face of that and other threats in cyberspace, CYBERCOM has sought to increase cyber defense funding in the region in recent years.

Subaru Tests Longtail WRX at the Nurburgring, but What Could It Be?
20 photos
Photo: Baldauf
The VB-series WRX came out in 2021. A whole bunch of limited editions and performance versions later, the VB could be on its way out. After all, the VA-series WRX came in 2014 and went the way of the dodo in 2021. The big question, however, is whether this black-painted test vehicle is a prototype of yet another VB performance version or a mule of its long-awaited replacement.
Spied testing with minimal camouflage at the world's most grueling racetrack, the mystery WRX appears to don extended rear quarter panels. Those panels extend outward, giving the car a particularly different look from the VB on sale today. A modified rear aerodynamic diffuser can also be seen, and the trunk lid is complemented by a very purposeful spoiler.
Why did Subaru camouflage it so carefully? The only answer to said question is future model development, though what kind of model remains to be seen. If you ask me, I believe that a new generation is on the horizon. The timing is right for such a move, and rather than coming up with a completely new platform, Subaru is much better off updating the current one.
Beyond the four-door sedan, the next generation is understood to be joined by a hatchback variant. The Japanese manufacturer previewed the hatchback at the 2025 Japan Mobility Show in the form of the Performance-B STI concept, a five-door show car loosely inspired by the hatchback-only Impreza.
Also worth noting, Subaru prepares to reveal the 2027 model year WRX for the Japanese domestic market. While not presented as an entirely new generation, the newcomer has been confirmed to feature an evolution of the heavy-duty STI manual transmission instead of the lesser TY75 box.
Photo: Baldauf Instead of cable operation, the TY85 is a rod-linked unit designed to handle more abuse and higher torque loads. A crack team of engineers discovered that a partner factory was still capable of building TY85 componentry, and that's how the manufacturer decided to revive this row-your-own tranny.
Said TY85-equipped WRX is one of three row-your-own models that Subaru will debut through 2027. The other two include a new version of the BRZ and a five-door hatchback. The latter is expected to be the WRX hatchback revival previewed by the 2025 Japan Mobility Show concept, and the hatchback should use the very same platform and oily bits as the TY85-equipped WRX.
Turning our attention back to the Nurburgring test vehicle, the camouflaged section of the diffuser extends farther rearward. The matching lip spoiler follows a completely new outline, reaching farther behind the trunk. Subaru also concealed the flat openings on either side of the rear bumper, making this vehicle all the more perplexing. All told, it looks like a longtail conversion of the VB.
Due to the lack of a ginormous rear wing and serious braking hardware, this definitely isn't an STI. The Japanese automaker confirmed back in March 2022 that the VB won't receive an STI variant, citing stricter regulations and the changing marketplace for its decision. At the time, Subaru further acknowledged that it's exploring opportunities, including electrification, for the next WRX STI.

source_document.body:
Mexican avocado producers have destroyed up to 52 tons of fruit after authorities detected a destructive agricultural pest in shipments intended for international export to the U.S. and other destinations.
The seed weevil pest raises concerns about potential disruptions to U.S.-Mexico avocado trade, which generates an estimated $641.5 million in cross-border transportation and warehousing activity.
Environmental officials in Michoacán, Mexico’s largest avocado-producing state, confirmed Sunday that avocado seed weevil larvae had been discovered in fruit destined for export, according to Reuters .
The discovery prompted authorities to detain shipments, while growers from Michoacán, Jalisco, Colima and Nayarit destroyed up to 52 tons of avocados over the weekend.
Mexico’s National Service of Health, Food Safety and Food Quality (SENASICA) supported the disposal of the fruit as part of efforts to prevent the pest from spreading.
Videos circulating on social media showed growers unloading truckloads of avocados into pits, where the fruit was burned and buried under pest-control protocols.
The avocado seed weevil can damage fruit by boring into its seed and can spread through orchards, threatening production if infestations are not contained.
Michoacán Environment Minister Alejandro Méndez confirmed the pest discovery to Reuters and said the potentially contaminated avocados had not entered commercial markets.
The incident comes at a sensitive time for Mexico’s avocado industry, which relies heavily on refrigerated trucking and cross-border distribution networks to supply U.S. grocery stores, restaurants and food distributors.
According to the U.S. Department of Agriculture , Mexico is forecast to export approximately 1.31 million metric tons of avocados worldwide in 2026, including roughly 1.2 million metric tons to the United States.
Michoacán and Jalisco are currently the only Mexican states authorized to export avocados to the U.S. market. Shipments must comply with phytosanitary requirements and inspections designed to prevent agricultural pests from entering the country.
The pest discovery follows other recent disruptions to Mexico’s avocado export industry.
In August, U.S. authorities temporarily suspended avocado export inspections in Michoacán following security concerns involving USDA personnel, interrupting shipments from the country’s largest production region, NBC reported .
More recently, avocado growers in Michoacán staged protests over low farm prices, disrupting harvesting and transportation operations. An Oct. 28 report by El País estimated that the demonstrations could reduce U.S.-bound avocado shipments from approximately 1,100 containers to 600 during the week.
The latest pest discovery adds another potential challenge for avocado exporters and the refrigerated trucking companies that transport produce from Mexican packinghouses to U.S. distribution centers.
Nearly 98% of Mexican avocados entering the U.S. in 2024 were transported by truck through Texas land ports, primarily through Pharr and Laredo .
Why it matters: Pest detections in Mexico’s avocado-producing regions could lead to additional inspections and shipment delays, potentially disrupting refrigerated trucking operations and the cross-border supply chain serving U.S. produce markets.

source_document.body:
By allowing compounding pharmacies to produce certain unapproved peptides, the Department of Health and Human Services could, in the short term, put patients in harm’s way. Longer term, the policy shift threatens the industry that brings new medicines to market.
Last week, the Department of Health and Human Services took the bold step of allowing the compounding of six unapproved peptide products. There are several reasons why this is a bad idea.
As a pharmacist, I strongly support compounding as an essential part of pharmacy practice. It serves patients whose needs cannot be met by commercially available medicines, including those with ingredient allergies or specific dosage requirements and those affected by legitimate shortages. I have defended that role in multiple comment letters to the FDA. But expanding commercial access to experimental peptides without adequate clinical evidence could put patients at risk, undermine confidence in legitimate compounding, and weaken incentives for rigorous drug development.
Nevertheless, the FDA and HHS have in recent months been moving toward broader access to compounded experimental peptides.
In July, FDA’s Pharmacy Compounding Advisory Committee (PCAC) recommended including six of seven peptides on the list of bulk substances permitted for traditional pharmacy compounding. On October 14, FDA submitted an interim peptide-access policy for White House review, and last week, the HHS released an interim enforcement discretion policy that, for all intents and purposes, allows the six unapproved peptides to be compounded and sold to consumers. Specifically, HHS said it does not intend to take enforcement action against state-licensed pharmacies, federal facilities, or licensed physicians compounding these peptides while FDA considers its final position.

Under the interim policy, officials do not intend to take action against sites that produce the peptides.

But the PCAC panel that voted in favor of allowing production of these peptides was stacked with professionals working in the peptide field, as overseen by Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr., who has championed broader access to peptides. Meanwhile, the FDA’s scientific reviewers recommended against all seven peptides , raising substantive concerns.
For BPC-157, they found insufficient evidence to establish effectiveness for ulcerative colitis . For KPV, they found no human clinical data to support its proposed uses. They also raised concerns about the substances’ identity and purity and their potential to trigger immune reactions. HHS now cites additional ingredient-testing data, historical use, and human-exposure information to justify its decision, but those materials should be evaluated against the specific evidence gaps the FDA staff scientists identified.
Moreover, peptide medicines already have an established path to FDA approval. Published reviews identify multiple FDA-approved peptide-based drugs, demonstrating that this pathway can bring these treatments to patients. That makes a transparent explanation of departures from the agency scientists’ conclusions especially important.
Indeed, the risks of unapproved peptides are drawing bipartisan scrutiny. In an Oct. 14 letter , a group of senators from both sides of the aisle urged the FDA to strengthen enforcement against online vendors selling unapproved drugs, including Eli Lilly’s next-gen obesity candidate retatrutide , under “research use only” labels, citing risks of contamination, mislabeling, and misuse.

Developing medicines, including peptide drugs, requires capital long before a product generates revenue. Investors finance studies that may fail, and developers must establish whether a treatment’s benefits justify its risks. Studies that find a treatment ineffective or reveal unacceptable risks protect patients even when no marketable medicine results.
Compounding rules should not create a competing route that makes those investments less worthwhile. If businesses can sell experimental peptides broadly without conducting comparable research, the incentive to fund that research could weaken. A policy that rewards early commercialization over evidence generation risks directing investment away from rigorous development and toward marketing. Patients could bear the consequences through fewer well-studied treatment options and persistent uncertainty.
The risk extends beyond the peptides under discussion. If HHS and FDA apply similar policies to other drug classes or disease areas because available treatments are inadequate, developers could face the same uncertainty across a much wider range of research programs. A company considering clinical development must assess whether it can sustain years of testing while competing with sellers already collecting revenue without the same obligations.
Widespread commercial access outside a trial could also make recruitment harder . Patients may choose a marketed product instead of participating in a study with eligibility rules, monitoring and a control group. That could further delay the evidence that responsible prescribing requires.
It is important that patients with serious or life-threatening illnesses not face avoidable delays in accessing investigational medicines. Clinical trials can provide eligible patients access to investigational treatments. When trial participation isn’t possible, and no satisfactory alternative exists, the FDA’s expanded access program , often called compassionate use, may permit treatment before approval. FDA, manufacturers, and research centers should make these pathways easier to navigate while protecting patients and preserving clinical research.
A policy that rewards early commercialization over evidence generation risks directing investment away from rigorous development.
Beyond the risks to patients and to the established research paradigm, broader compounding access also creates opportunities for abuse. Traditional compounding pharmacies are regulated, primarily by states , but their products do not undergo FDA premarket approval. Although qualifying compounded drug products are exempt from federal current good manufacturing practice requirements, HHS policy requires the original bulk-ingredient manufacturer to comply. Compounders must also test ingredients, obtain patient-specific prescriptions, and report serious adverse events and product quality issues to the FDA and relevant states.
HHS argues that this approach offers patients a more controlled alternative to illicit online sellers. Licensed pharmacies may offer better quality control, but quality testing and adverse-event reporting cannot replace clinical studies that establish whether a peptide works and whether its benefits outweigh its risks. In addition, permission to compound a substance should not be marketed as FDA approval or proof of safety and effectiveness.
HHS and FDA should explain how expanded access will preserve incentives for clinical research. Regulators should verify compliance with the policy’s sourcing, testing, and reporting conditions and ensure patients receive clear disclosures about the products’ unapproved status. FDA and state regulators must enforce the distinction between legitimate compounding and businesses using the classification to evade manufacturing or approval requirements. That includes action against exaggerated therapeutic claims and operations that disguise routine commercial production as individualized care.
I have consistently argued that consumer demand and business preference cannot substitute for clinical need. The same principle applies here. Compounding should remain available for patients who need it while public policy supports the research that can turn promising molecules into treatments patients can trust.

source_document.body:
The cessation of manufacturing activities follows a Sun Pharma recall and reports that regulators found fault with the company’s quality system.
Sun Pharmaceutical Industries has stopped manufacturing eye-care drugs at a plant in India amid quality concerns.
On an earnings call Friday, Sun Pharma Managing Director Kirti Ganorkar told investors that the company “voluntarily recalled” 11 ophthalmology products and “voluntarily initiated a temporary cessation” of manufacturing activities. However, on the same day, Reuters reported that Indian drug regulators had ordered Sun Pharma to stop manufacturing ophthalmic products at the facility after finding quality management system failures.
Indian regulators reportedly ordered Sun Pharma to shut down its facility in the Indian state of Assam on Aug. 20. The order followed a joint federal-state inspection that identified problems with Sun Pharma’s system for ensuring quality and safety, Reuters said.
Sun Pharma has “taken a remedial action so that we can put everything in place shortly,” Ganorkar said on the earnings call. Indian regulators are reportedly reviewing a compliance report that Sun Pharma submitted in response to the order to stop production.
The company voluntarily recalled 11 ophthalmic products from the Indian market in July. Sun Pharma’s notice lacked an explanation for the recall. However, it later emerged that the All India Ophthalmological Society (AIOS) alerted its members in June about the bacterial contamination of batches of Sun Pharma’s Predmet eye drops.
Multiple ophthalmic institutions found contamination consistent with the presence of Pseudomonas , a pathogen that was responsible for a U.S. eye infection outbreak in 2022 and 2023. In that outbreak, 14 patients who used artificial tears sold by EzriCare and Delsam Pharma suffered vision loss. Indian drugmaker Global Pharma manufactured the EzriCare and Delsam artificial tears.
Sun Pharma has yet to publish a statement about the shutdown, with its public comments limited to a line in the Reuters article and Ganorkar’s response to an analyst’s question on the earnings call. India’s the Bombay Stock Exchange asked Sun Pharma to provide clarification after viewing the Reuters report.
